Six units at Nouvel 18, New Futura linked to money laundering case head to auction
article:
Four units at freehold development Nouvel 18 in District 10 and a four-bedder at New Futura along Leonie Hill Road will be going under the hammer at SRI’s upcoming auction on Oct 28.

The properties are among the assets forfeited in Singapore’s $3 billion money laundering case.

In late August, Deloitte Singapore said more than 1,000 luxury items, including jewellery, watches and handbags, as well as 80 real estate properties forfeited in Singapore’s $3 billion money laundering case, would be auctioned in phases between September 2026 and mid-2027.

Deloitte was appointed by the Singapore police last year to manage and realise the non-cash assets seized in connection to the money laundering case.

The latest properties come on the back of 10 apartments at Martin Modern and Wallich Residences that were put on the block in September. Four apartments — two from each development — were successfully sold at auction , with prices ranging from $2.08 million to $6.6 million.

Five luxury apartments at Nouvel 18 up for auction

The five residences at Nouvel 18 are priced from $2,939 psf to $3,558 psf. They comprise four unit types — two- and three-bedroom + study units, and three- and five-bedders — ranging from 1,335 to 6,125 sq ft.

Located in the exclusive Ardmore Park area, Nouvel 18 houses 156 units across two 36-storey residential blocks. It was completed in 2014 and includes facilities such as a swimming pool, BBQ clubhouse, gym, tennis court, and concierge service for its residents.

The freehold luxury development along Anderson Road is about a five-minute drive away from retail and lifestyle amenities at the Orchard Road shopping belt.

“With five units being offered at auction, buyers have multiple opportunities to secure a freehold residence within a development that offers privacy, comprehensive facilities and close proximity to Orchard Road,” said Mok Sze Sze, managing partner of SRI Auction.

Four-bedder at New Futura on the block

In District 9, the four-bedroom unit at New Futura spans 2,691 sq ft with a guide price of $9.8 million, or $3,642 psf.

Mok added that the home’s “generous layout” offers substantial living space for families seeking a home in Singapore’s established prime residential districts.

New Futura is a 124-unit freehold condominium completed in 2017. It is within a 10-minute walk of Somerset MRT Station, with a range of lifestyle, dining and retail amenities nearby at Great World and along Orchard Road at Cineleisure, 111 Somerset , and Ngee Ann City .

The auction for the units at Nouvel 18 and New Futura will take place at 2.30 pm on Oct 28 at SRI’s Great World office.

title: Get Smart: Interest Rates Hiked, Are S-REITs Doomed to Mediocrity?
article:
It finally happened.
The US Federal Reserve
raised interest rates
by 0.25% on 16 September 2026.
More increases have been signalled.
S-REITs, which have spent six difficult years adjusting to
higher borrowing costs
, now face the question again: can they cope with another round of rate hikes?
Many will remember the damage interest rates inflicted on S-REITs two years ago.
It begs the question: are S-REITs doomed to mediocrity again?
The answer depends less on where rates end up and more on how quickly they get there.
Did REITs cope with the last round of gradual hikes?
Between 2015 and 2018, the Fed raised rates in 0.25% increments over a three-to-four-year period.
The increases were predictable and spaced out.
Many S-REITs grew their distribution per unit (DPU) throughout that entire cycle.
For instance,
Mapletree Logistics Trust
(SGX: M44U), or MLT, raised its DPU from S$0.075 in its financial year ended 31 March 2015 (FY15) to S$0.07941 in FY19.
And MLT isn’t the only one.
The same can be said of
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U) and
Parkway Life REIT
(SGX: C2PU).
Tellingly, all three are from different industries.
There is a reason why these REITs were able to do so, in our eyes.
REITs operate under long-term contracts on both sides of their balance sheet.
Their tenants sign multi-year leases.
Their lenders extend loans with fixed maturity dates.
A REIT cannot walk into its bank tomorrow and refinance every loan, nor can it approach its tenants mid-lease and demand higher rents.
It is bound by what it has already signed.
Gradual rate hikes give REITs time to work within these constraints.
As leases expire, they renew at higher rents that reflect the new rate environment.
As loans mature, they refinance at whatever rate the market offers.
The income side and the cost side adjust in parallel, and the REIT absorbs the change without squeezing its distributions.
Why did the 2022-2023 cycle catch REITs off guard?
In contrast, the
rate-hike cycle
that began in 2022 was not gradual.
It was the steepest increase in roughly 35 years.
Between March 2022 and July 2023, the US federal funds rate climbed from near zero to 5.5% in under two years.
That steep increase left almost no room for adjustment.
REITs were locked into existing leases that reflected a near-zero rate world.
Their floating-rate loans repriced immediately at far higher costs, while their rental income stayed flat until leases came up for renewal.
The mismatch between fast-rising costs and slow-moving revenue squeezed DPUs across the sector.
The damage showed up in earnings over 2024 and 2025, when higher borrowing costs started to bite into distributable income.
Very few S-REITs came through this period with their DPU intact.
A handful managed to grow distributions every single year from 2020 through to today — a stretch that included a pandemic, tariff disruptions, and the sharpest rate spike in a generation.
They were the exception, not the norm.
Where do rates sit today?
The current US federal funds rate sits at around 4%.
That is higher in the pre-2022 world, but it remains 1.5 percentage points below the 2023–2024 peak of 5.5%.
This gap matters for REITs in a specific way.
Any loan taken out or refinanced near the 2023–2024 peak can now be renewed at a lower rate, even after the latest increase.
S-REITs that locked in borrowing at those elevated levels would actually see their interest costs fall when they next refinance, as long as rates stay below 5.5%.
The risk is not today’s rate level.
Instead, the risk is whether the Fed’s signalled increases come gradually or steeply.
A measured path from 4% to 5%, spread over two years with predictable 0.25% steps, gives REITs the same adjustment window that made 2015–2018 manageable.
A rapid march back towards 5.5% in under a year would recreate the same mismatch that hurt the sector in 2022 and 2023.
Get Smart: It’s about pacing
When rates rise, the reaction is to ask whether your REIT can survive higher borrowing costs.
That question skips the refinancing cycle that is more important.
REITs do not fail because rates are high.
They get squeezed when rates rise faster than their leases and loans can adjust.
The next time the Fed signals a hike, check your REIT’s weighted average debt maturity and lease expiry profile.
A REIT with well-staggered maturities on both sides of its balance sheet may be able to digest gradual increases without cutting its DPU.

title: Singapore sees Southeast Asia thriving amid ‘breakdown’ of world order
article:
(Oct 7): Singapore’s top diplomat touted what he called “a moment of great potential” for Southeast Asia, as economies expand rapidly on surging technology demand even as much of the world faces growing uncertainties.

Speaking during a conference on Wednesday, Minister for Foreign Affairs Vivian Balakrishnan said semiconductors and artificial intelligence (AI) were major drivers helping the region’s economies outperform expectations. He noted that the city-state expanded 6.1% in the first half of the year, with Taiwan overtaking China to become its biggest trading partner.

“In the midst of a crazy world, in the midst of the breakdown in world order, the breakdown in trade, the disruption to supply chains, we’re having significant growth,” he said. “In fact, to the point where you start having to worry — why is it so high?”

Asia’s powerhouse economies have seized the lion’s share of trade growth in the global AI boom, because they make the chips and other equipment needed for data centres springing up around the globe. The World Bank cites several Asian economies that have outpaced expectations on high-tech exports, with Vietnam expected to grow 7.4% in 2026, Indonesia 5.2% and Malaysia 5.1%.

Singapore’s electronics exports surged 132% in August from a year earlier, and the island nation has upgraded its 2026 economic growth forecast to between 4.5%-5.5%. Vietnam and Malaysia have likewise strengthened their roles in electronics supply chains as firms spread production across more locations.

See also: Central banks should have a ‘prudently hawkish bias’: IMF chief

But the World Bank has also warned that the region’s dependence on AI-related industry could become a weakness if global investment in the technology slows.

Balakrishnan acknowledged the risks posed by the technology itself, saying “loss of control is a real threat”. He also said rogue states and non-state actors could use AI to develop new forms of disruption, including in chemistry, biology and weapons of mass destruction.

Still, with Singapore set to chair the regional bloc known as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations next year, the diplomat said the region should use the momentum to deepen economic integration.

See also: Yellen says Trump ‘appalling’ on US allies, backs retaliation

“This is a moment of great potential and peril,” Balakrishnan said — later adding: “There’s also a lot of money to be made.”

title: Central banks should have a ‘prudently hawkish bias’: IMF chief
article:
International Monetary Fund (IMF) managing director Kristalina Georgieva is no stranger to the dangers of inflation. In the mid-1990s, the Bulgarian national watched her country go through a period of hyperinflation.

Inflation soared to 8,300%, wiping out the savings of almost all Bulgarians, including Georgieva’s own mother. Fortunately, Bulgaria’s government took tough but necessary policy actions to remedy the situation. Fast forward to today and Bulgaria’s income per capita has gone up eight times and it became a member of the European Union in 2007.

Witnessing that episode left Georgieva with a heightened awareness of what inflation could do to economies if left unattended. What happened to Bulgaria can happen elsewhere, and right now it is the global economy at large that is grappling with inflation.

“The AI building boom is inflationary. The energy and food shocks are inflationary. Tariffs, defence spending, and high public debt can be inflationary. And memories of the recent high inflation are still fresh,” Georgieva said in her curtain raiser speech for the IMF’s upcoming annual meetings on Oct 7. Georgieva delivered her speech at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy in Singapore, a week before the meetings are slated to commence in Bangkok, Thailand.

Inflation itself has become sticky. In the US, inflation has exceeded the Federal Reserve’s (Fed) target of 2% for more than five years. But that did not stop the Federal Reserve from cutting interest rates in December 2025 by 25 basis points to between 3.5% and 3.75%.

“We draw comfort from long-term inflation expectations staying anchored, but let us not forget the simple fact that inflation is only anchored until it is not. I learned the hard way from Bulgaria’s hyperinflation, this lesson,” Georgieva says.

See also: Yellen says Trump ‘appalling’ on US allies, backs retaliation

“Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries’ monetary policy. It is highly appropriate that the US Federal Reserve, the ECB (European Central Bank), and the Bank of Japan have all raised rates and spoken firmly, with future policy rate paths repricing accordingly.”

With an end to the Iran war nowhere in sight, policymakers have begun to accept that higher energy prices are here to stay. Even the newly minted Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who had chosen to hold rates steady after taking office in May, had to do an about-face. The Federal Open Market Committee announced on Sept 16 that it had voted unanimously to hike rates by 25 basis points to 3.75% and 4%. Market watchers and analysts are now forecasting at least one more rate hike by the end of this year.

See also: Ray Dalio warns China, Japan may pull back from US Treasuries

Asia’s economy has grown by leaps and bounds over the past few decades. According to the IMF’s data, Asia Pacific’s share of global GDP is now at 43% today, up from 25% in 1991.

Georgieva, however, warns in her speech that it could be much harder to sustain global economic growth in the coming years. This is because of three major crosscurrents that are disrupting the world today: the rise of AI, high energy prices and soaring public debt levels.

“To put it simply, the global economy is being pulled in two opposite directions: a negative energy supply shock on the energy side and a positive demand shock from AI,” she says. “The combined impact of these two forces is highly uneven across the world.”

Georgieva expects global investment-to-GDP in AI to surpass the amounts that went into earlier industrial booms, such as the construction of the railroad, electricity grid or telecommunication network. In fact, AI hardware and related products already account for more than 10% of the world’s goods trade and is still rising, she adds.

That said, AI consumes a lot of energy and will add pressure to the present energy shock caused by the war in Iran. Prices of Brent crude continue to trade at around US$100 per barrel and a structural shortfall in refining capacity are sending prices of diesel and other refined products to record highs, Georgieva says.

“To quote from Game of Thrones, winter is coming. Price pressures may build further as countries replenish reserves and demand rises with the approach of the Northern hemisphere cold season. Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, high energy prices would likely persist for some time. Brent futures, for example, now predict high oil prices through 2027.”

Higher energy prices have knock on effects too, pushing up inflation, interest rates and benchmark yields. This will add even more pressure to the fiscal crunch that advanced economies like the US and Japan are already grappling with. Global public debt is on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP and is nearing levels not seen since after World War II, Georgieva says.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

While some policymakers might be counting on AI to help spur growth, Georgieva cautions against such complacency. The capital-intensive nature of AI has caused Big Tech companies to turn to the debt and equity markets to fund their investments. Bond issuances by hyperscalers will thus be competing against sovereign bond issuances for capital.

“Policymakers had a relatively easy ride over the last 17 years as for all that time interest rates were stuck below GDP growth rates,” Georgieva says. “Now, it is no more the case.”

To best address this, Georgieva urges heavily indebted, advanced countries to lower their reliance on monetary policy. Instead, such countries need to focus on fiscal consolidation and pursue broader structural reforms to revive their economies. This applies to emerging markets as well who should be trying to expand their fiscal space and foreign exchange buffers.

“Fiscal consolidation will be a heavy lift,” Georgieva says. “After a succession of shocks where, each time, fiscal policy has had to step in to cushion the impact, people have grown accustomed to state support, and yet some very tough political choices stare us in the face.”

title: Temasek chief investment officer says AI, inflation pose biggest market risks in 2027
article:
(Oct 7): Temasek International’s investment chief highlighted the potential for the artificial intelligence (AI) trade to reverse and inflation pushing up bond rates to a point that may end the runup for equities as top risks facing global markets heading into next year.

“The unwinding of the AI trade is the biggest risk,” said Temasek International chief investment officer Rohit Sipahimalani. “We don’t see that as imminent. But, will you have bumps in 2027, possibly yes.”

Speaking at the Milken Asia Summit 2026 in Singapore on Wednesday, Sipahimalani said the other main issue is “concerns around inflation”.

“Inflation is a risk, together with what is happening in the rates environment, that means there probably is a risk of some breaking point in the equity market at some point,” he said. Together with AI, these are “two key risks I would see for 2027”.

Debate is raging ahead of the upcoming US earnings season that will mark a key test of whether hundreds of billions of dollars of AI-related spending by tech giants is following through to stronger profits. Global bonds have slumped as higher energy prices and fiscal borrowing needs push bets on more central bank rate hikes to rein in inflation.

State-owned Temasek, which had $518 billion as of March 31, this year pledged to more than double its allocation to AI-related investments from 6% to up to 15% by 2031. AI has already been a major driver of the firm’s returns — it owns stakes in some of the sector’s biggest names including OpenAI, Anthropic and Nvidia Corp.

See also: Asian stocks hold near record highs, oil climbs

Sipahimalani on Wednesday said he wants to move more of that AI exposure away from private holdings into publicly traded assets. This will help Temasek remain nimble to respond timely if needed, he said.

“AI is such a fast changing environment, things could change quite easily and you have to be able to pivot,” he said.

The firm has around half its AI exposure in public markets, and “we want to increase that number ideally to 70% to 75% so it gives us more flexibility to pivot with changes in the environment, as against being stuck with a private asset which there’s little you can do when things are changing”, he added.

See also: Asia stocks rise after US tech rally, oil steadies

Temasek’s investments in the Americas have surged in recent years, thanks in large part to AI investments, and made up 26% of its portfolio as of March 31.

Speaking on the same panel at the Milken event, Mubadala chief financial officer Carlos Obeid said the Middle Eastern fund has been trying diligently over the last few years to increase its Asia exposure.

“A few years ago, the share of the portfolio that was allocated or invested in Asia was about 10%, it has increased now to about 13% and we want to do more,” he said. “We’ve been present in China mainly, South Korea, Japan and India. And we want to grow those exposures.”

Granite Asia Capital senior managing partner Jenny Lee on the same panel highlighted how the narrrative has changed for allocators’ investing in China.

“I think China has gone from ‘China is not investable’ to ‘Is China investable’ with a question mark to now the most common question I get — ‘are we missing out?’,” she said.

title: Topix’s biggest ever revamp to cull hundreds of Japan stocks
article:
(Oct 7): Japan Exchange Group Inc unveiled the biggest-ever reshuffle of the Topix on Wednesday, a revamp that shrinks one of Asia’s broadest major equity benchmarks and intensifies pressure on Japanese companies to boost their market appeal.

There were 683 companies earmarked for removal under tougher inclusion rules, according to JPX’s announcement. Those slated for gradual removal include Medley Inc and Ichiyoshi Securities Co. Among the 35 stocks that will be added are McDonald’s Holdings Co Japan and Ferrotec Corp. The changes will begin to take effect on Oct 30.

The changes are the second stage of a multiyear effort by the group, which operates the Tokyo Stock Exchange, to make the Topix more investable. The benchmark has long stood out among major global indexes for its large number of constituents, including hundreds of relatively illiquid small-cap companies.

The overhaul has potentially significant implications for global investors. About ¥166 trillion (RM4.3 trillion) in passive assets track the Topix, according to a September estimate by Daiwa Securities chief quantitative analyst Junichi Hashimoto. Companies that are to be dropped face rules-driven selling by index funds while those pencilled for inclusion can generate steady demand from passive investors and will be on the radar of active managers seeking to beat the index.

The first phase of the revamp that ended in January 2025 reduced the number of members to about 1,700 from roughly 2,200. After the latest overhaul, the tally could fall further to just under 1,000 in two years. Cutting the number of constituents should make it easier for investors to run passive strategies tracking the index while encouraging competition among aspiring companies to secure a place in the benchmark.

See also: Suzuki undercuts BYD as competition for cheap mini EVs heats up

Reducing Topix constituents is “basically positive", said Hiromi Ishihara, head of equity investment at Amundi Japan Ltd. As companies increasingly need to justify their inclusion in the index and “if steady reforms at individual companies add up, the Japanese equity market as a whole could gain a higher valuation,” she said.

Ishihara said there have been several cases in which small-cap companies stepped up shareholder returns in an effort to avoid removal from the Topix, helping to lift their share prices. For investors, she said, there are opportunities in determining “whether actions aimed at staying in the index end up being temporary measures to support the share price or lead to genuine increases in corporate value through stronger corporate governance and other reforms.”

Under the new rules, additions and deletions will be determined using criteria including annual traded-value turnover, a measure of how actively shares change hands and the market capitalisation of shares available to public investors.

Stocks selected for removal will not disappear from the index immediately. Their weightings will be reduced quarterly through July 2028. Companies that meet the requirements when they are reassessed in October 2027 can halt that process. From October 2028, the benchmark will be rebalanced annually.

Investors are expected to remain mindful of the risk that small-cap stocks could be removed from Topix going forward and “the trend toward large-cap stocks will likely strengthen”, said Shota Sando, an analyst at Tokai Tokyo Intelligence Lab.

title: Ray Dalio says we’re nearing point where AI bubble may burst
article:
(Oct 7): Billionaire Ray Dalio warned that artificial intelligence (AI) is a “classic bubble” that is nearing a bursting point thanks to rising interest rates and the need to turn wealth into cash.

Speaking at the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore on Wednesday, Dalio said that a huge amount of debt is being taken out to fund AI. As rates continue to climb, that is a point at which the bubble begins to pop.

“We’re in the part of the cycle that is before that but approaching that,” the Bridgewater founder said. “I think we’re close to that.”

His comments come as technology giants spend hundreds of billions of dollars on AI, increasingly financed with debt, and as market gains concentrate in a handful of stocks. Bond yields around the world have surged to the highest in decades, increasing the cost of funding the enormous investment needed to build AI infrastructure.

Still, equity valuations continue to rise, with optimism over technology earnings propelling the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 indices to record highs this week.

Dalio, who has long warned of an AI bubble, said there were other issues that could trigger its collapse. Those include wealth taxes and other efforts to convert unrealised gains into cash.

See also: Nvidia’s valuations show AI rally isn’t a bubble, DBS says

“Everybody says ‘I’m worth a billion dollars’ but OK, try to spend that,” he added. “In order to spend that you have to sell wealth in order to get money — and so the bubble usually pricks at that.”

title: Copper stable as AI-driven tech stock rally holds near record
article:
(Oct 7): Copper steadied as a rally in tech-related stocks held near record highs, driven by optimism about the artificial intelligence boom.

Contracts on the London Metal Exchange were little changed on Wednesday, reflecting broader caution across other markets. The red metal is set to receive a demand boost from data centres built for the AI industry, the same sector driving this week’s gains in global stocks.

The copper market is still in consolidation mode after surging to a record last month when the threat of US tariffs on refined metal prompted a rush of supplies to America, tightening it elsewhere. Traders are awaiting the reopening of markets in China, the world’s top metal consumer, following a week-long national holiday for the next cues on price direction.

Copper futures were steady at US$14,413 a tonne on the LME at 9.55am Singapore time. Aluminium was 0.4% higher while zinc added 0.1%.

title: US court allows fund to obtain documents in Radiant World case
article:
(Oct 7): A US court has allowed a fund managed by Mariner Investment Group to obtain documents from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the Clearing House Interbank Payments System in its Swiss proceedings against iron ore trader Radiant World, according to an order.

Judge John P Cronan of the US District Court for the Southern District of New York allowed the request made by Mariner Atlantic Multi-Strategy LLC, ordering it to provide copies of the decision to all targets. These include Radiant World, group founder Pinkesh Nahar and director Bhupeshkumar Gejvala, as well as related entity Sapphire Minmetals.

The fund has accused Radiant World of fraud and money laundering, and has asked Swiss prosecutors to open a criminal investigation, conduct searches of company premises and seize bank accounts and other assets.

A Radiant World spokesperson had no immediate comment. Mariner did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside business hours.

Radiant World is facing a spate of civil lawsuits from Singapore to London over allegations from creditors that it provided banks with falsified documents to secure financing, while Singapore Police are also conducting an investigation into the company. The company’s main offices are located in Singapore, Switzerland and Dubai.

See also: Korean investors suffer US$1.7 bil losses from leveraged ETFs

title: Beware of stranded assets when data centre boom ‘finally fizzles out’: Ho Kwon Ping
article:
Southeast Asian countries should be wary of the rapid data centre build-out, lest they become stuck with “the most stranded assets” when the data centre boom “finally fizzles out”, says Ho Kwon Ping, founder and executive chairman of Banyan Group.

Speaking at the opening panel of the Forbes Global CEO Conference on Oct 7, Ho warns that some regional markets may be focused on the “immediacy of data centres in terms of what it can do for the investors”, adding that the new-builds offer “not much employment generation”.

“I think we need to have a little bit more of a sceptical look about the proliferation of data centres across Asia, rather than everybody seeing that this is the latest big thing that we should all jump into,” he says.

Ho believes this proliferation echoes the manufacturing boom in Southeast Asia “30 years ago”, when corporates set up factories in the region to produce goods like disc drives. “It’s the same thing — outsourcing to the developing world the most basic AI work, the basic learning and so on.”

Ho also points to the “economics of data centres”. “Most of the data centres that are being set up around Asia are in fact by large funds, where a lot of people have invested into the private equity companies that are making a lot of money, and they’re only contracted to sell to the AI companies themselves with contracts [that] are relatively easy to break. I’m just waiting to see, when this data centre boom finally fizzles out, which country is going to be left with the most stranded assets.”

Discussions around AI are often conflated with the investment boom in AI-related infrastructure. “There’s actually two completely separate threads,” says Ho. “The best parallel to this is the US railroad boom and bust in the 19th century. [It] led to a lot of extremely positive things, [such as the] opening up of all of the US, [but] it also led to a lot of stranded railways all across the US.”

See also: Singapore-based data centre operator BDx breaks ground for an AI data centre in Java

Ho urges caution around the “current boom”. “It’s going to lead to a physical and investment bust, while the rest of the technology continues to benefit the world. It’s two separate issues we should be talking about.”

Further, Ho believes the “weaponisation of AI” is “most likely the next big danger to the world”. “My cynical view when you talk about regulation is that I don’t think you’re going to get China, the US or any country in the world coming together very nicely to talk about regulating AI until some very, very bad intentional or unintentional accident happens.”

Given the current “arms race” between nations over developing AI, however, “it’s kind of fanciful or delusional” to believe companies will “exercise self-restraint” and prioritise the greater good, says V Shankar, co-founder and CEO of Singapore and Dubai-based alternative investment manager Gateway Partners.

See also: New data centres worth US$68 billion disrupted in US, data show

Speaking on the same panel, Shankar says it remains to be seen if the current build-out of data centres is “similar to the fibre optic subsea [cables], where there was huge overcapacity, or is it [similar to] a cloud build-out, where there has not been overcapacity and has actually turned out pretty well”.

Staying on those examples, PwC global chairman Mohamed Kande says the value of these Internet-enabling infrastructure were not found in their build-out or supply, but in the diffusion and adoption of the Internet by users. “It was the adoption of the internet that made a difference, not the supply of the internet.”

Kande adds: “The same thing is going to happen. The societies and the companies that are going to rise [and] benefit from all of this investment in AI — not only companies but societies — are the ones that are going to diffuse and adopt AI at scale.”

title: 韩国生物医学公司NEXT&BIO 计划扩大新加坡研发团队
达利欧：当前市场已近泡沫破裂节点
